stem:
A 58-year-old is ventilated in ICU after return of spontaneous circulation following an out-of-hospital VF arrest. To blow off the acidosis, the team has increased the ventilator rate. He has no chronic lung disease. Blood pressure is 102/60 mmHg on low-dose noradrenaline.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pH | 7.29 | 7.35–7.45 |
| PaCO2 | 28 mmHg | 35–45 |
| Bicarbonate | 13 mmol/L | 22–28 |
| Lactate | 7.5 mmol/L | 0.5–2.0 |
| PaO2 (FiO2 0.4) | 105 mmHg | — |

What ventilation change is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the rate further to correct the pH
options.explanation: Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and can worsen brain ischaemia after arrest; the metabolic acidosis should resolve with restored perfusion, not be corrected by overventilation.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the current rate until lactate clears
options.explanation: A PaCO2 of 28 mmHg is already low enough to reduce cerebral blood flow; keeping it there while waiting for lactate to clear risks secondary brain injury.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce minute ventilation to a PaCO2 of 35–45
options.explanation: After return of circulation, ANZCOR advises targeting normocapnia (PaCO2 35–45 mmHg) to avoid hypocapnic cerebral vasoconstriction. Reduce minute ventilation and correct the acidosis by restoring perfusion.

options.label: D
options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate and keep the current rate
options.explanation: Bicarbonate is not routinely recommended for post-arrest metabolic acidosis, and it does not correct the harmful hypocapnia.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure and worsens acidosis; without chronic CO2 retention, normocapnia is the target.

context: After cardiac arrest, ventilate to normocapnia (PaCO2 35–45 mmHg); hypocapnia worsens brain ischaemia even when it partly corrects a metabolic acidosis.
